newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU scientists to examine UK certified herd scheme.
newsitem.headline: EU scientists to examine UK certified herd scheme.

text.p: European Union scientists are due to examine a proposal to allow exports of British cattle from herds certified to be free of mad cow disease, the first step in lifting a worldwide ban on British beef.
Britain sent the proposal to EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler on Tuesday, saying it had now met the five preconditions for lifting the ban agreed at the EU Council in Florence in June 1996.

After a delay of several months pending examination of a study on maternal transmission of the disease and cull options, Britain is due to start in early March the selective slaughter of around an extra 100,000 extra animals believed to be at risk of catching mad cow disease -- bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).

The selective slaughter scheme was the final precondition agreed in Florence. Britain is implementing the other four: - animal identification and movement recording - removal of meat and bone meal from feed mills and farms - slaughter and destruction of animals over 30 months of age - stricter controls on removal of the spinal cord and other risky tissue from carcases.

Under the proposed certified herds scheme, beef would only be exported from: - animals under 30 months old, in which there was no trace of infection even in the central nervous tissues. - animals which had not been exposed to infection either in the herd in which they were born or in any other herd in which they had been present.

Exports of meat and products would have to meet the following conditions: - The animal must be clearly identifiable throughout its life. - The animal was not over 30 months of age at slaughter. - Absence for at least six years of confirmed or suspect cases of BSE in cattle born in the animal's natal herd and in cattle in herds which it has subsequently entered. - The animal was slaughtered separately from uncertified animals and its meat kept apart.
The proposal also gives details on the issue of certificates and control at and after slaughter in Northern Ireland and in Britain, where officials do not have direct access to abattoirs.

Britain said that although no member state can provide an absolute assurance that an animal has not been exposed to the BSE agent, the scientifically based proposal places British beef "on a basis at least as secure as beef from other member states."
